confirmed: Read the entire supplied markdown, including all supplementary material, and checked the recorded numbers against PDF text/tables and the rendered figures. The source is the 84-page arXiv preprint supplied under record 2412.03151; its metadata creation date is 2024-12-04 and no version number is printed. Main text ends on p. 29; supplementary materials occupy pp. 30-84 (PDF metadata; pp. 1, 29-30, 84).
The title and all nine author names match the document. The supplement explicitly lists Supplementary Text, Tables S1-S22, and Figs. S1-S8 (PDF pp. 1 and 30).

ai_vs_human is the correct design and context class, and core = no is correct. People completed an admission assessment; the models independently answered its tasks. The sole random assignment of people was to Test A or B, not to AI assistance, and the collective-creativity groups are resampled response pools (PDF pp. 14, 21-24).

The overall human sample is 467 people in China: 330 female, 137 male, age 21-53, mean 27.56, SD 6.03, all with at least a Bachelor’s degree; 103 were current students and 140 current employees. These are people, not response or rating counts (PDF pp. 6 and 21).

Human analyzed counts vary by task: Divergent Thinking Task 1 n = 230, Scientific Problem Solving Task 3 n = 237, Creative Advert Writing n = 418, and keyword-writing diversity n = 178. The first two analyses cover the respective test-form samples, supporting the overall human sample count while distinguishing it from each outcome denominator (PDF p. 21 and Table S4, pp. 39-42).

The battery contains 13 tasks across divergent thinking, problem solving, and creative writing, distributed between two test forms. Task limits are 5 minutes for divergent thinking and adverts, 7 minutes for problem-solving and emoji-writing tasks, and 10 + 10 minutes for keyword writing (PDF pp. 19-21).

The five model names and versions, API versus web-portal use, and GPT temperature range 0-1 match the form. Two rating rounds used five psychology-student raters per round, source-blind response lists, invalid-response screening, mean ratings, and z-score linear equating (PDF pp. 22-23).

S1-O1 reported numbers match: average percentile 46th; Claude and GPT-4 52nd, SparkDesk 44th, Qwen 42nd, GPT-3.5 37th; domain means 55th, 59th, and 25th. The form correctly notes the paper’s internal discrepancy: the Discussion instead says GPT-3.5 38th (PDF pp. 8 and 17).

S1-O2 matches Table S4: GPT-4 M = 1.562, SD = 0.143, n = 41; human M = 2.29, SD = 0.612, n = 418; 95% CI of the difference [-0.801, -0.654], t = -19.496, df = 239.107, P < 0.001, Cohen’s d = -1.242. The five model effects span -1.765 to -1.242; n_units = 459 combines model and human outputs, not people. The additional keyword-creativity d = 1.416 also matches (PDF pp. 41-42, Table S4).

S1-O3 matches Table S6: keyword writing has 402 LLM stories and 399 human stories, 80601 and 79401 pairs, cosine similarities 0.907 and 0.870, and Levenshtein distances 0.897 and 0.922. n_units = 160002 is the sum of the two printed pair counts, not a participant count; no inferential test is shown. The embedding model is text-embedding-ada-002 (PDF p. 24 and p. 49, Table S6; story counts also in Table S1, p. 33).

S1-O4 matches Table S4: GPT-4 M = 2.85, SD = 0.534, n = 50; human M = 3.301, SD = 0.678, n = 178; 95% CI of the difference [-0.656, -0.247], t = -4.346, df = 226, P < 0.001, Cohen’s d = -0.696. The 228 units combine model and human two-story responses. Coding this within-response comparison as flexibility is consistent with the codebook (PDF p. 20 and p. 41, Table S4).

S1-O5 figure labels match exactly: GPT-4 10.42, Claude 9.99, SparkDesk 8.66, Qwen 8.64, and GPT-3.5 7.71 equivalent humans. The procedure uses 1000 resamples per human group size and five groups of ten model responses; top-response ties are retained. These are bootstrap-based equivalences, not numbers of people assigned to intervention arms (PDF pp. 13-15, Fig. 6 inspected).

The collective-creativity statement that LLMs supply approximately 33% of the top responses matches the text; the incremental slope 0.52 and intercept 3.41 match the Mixed LLMs line in Fig. 7, subject to the scope correction above (PDF p. 13, Table S11 on p. 58, and Fig. 7 on p. 16 inspected).

The one-line finding’s numerical claims are supported. Humans have the lowest cosine similarity and highest Levenshtein distance on every task in Table S6; the percentile and equivalent-human ranges match the cited main-text results and figure (PDF p. 8; Fig. 6, p. 15; Table S6, pp. 48-49).

This is an original benchmarking study, not a synthesis; leaving pooled meta-analysis fields at their defaults is appropriate. Its literature comparison table does not constitute an additional randomized-people study conducted in this paper (PDF pp. 3-6 and 19-24).
summary: The AI-versus-human classification and reported numbers are supported; no study randomized people to AI assistance. Corrections concern incomplete coding, test-form counts, outcome coverage and descriptions, company involvement, and the data link.
